title: "Fitting ecological response curves"
---

```{r}
#| include: false
# Load ggplot2 for the consistently formatted rendered figures in this chapter.
library(ggplot2)
```

# Introduction

In this chapter, we learn how to fit an ecological response curve to data: a deterministic
function of a predictor describes one parameter of the distribution of each observation
(usually its mean), and the parameters of the function are estimated by maximum likelihood.
Once the curve is fitted, we estimate the uncertainty of its parameters and of the curve
itself, check whether the fitted model describes the data, revise the model where it does
not, and compare it with alternative models.

The chapter brings together the two pillars of the book, probability distributions and
likelihood ([Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd) to [Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd))
and deterministic functions ([Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd)). What is new is the
likelihood of a response curve, in which every observation has a distribution of its own;
how RTMB calculates the gradient of the negative log-likelihood that the optimiser uses;
the uncertainty of a fitted curve; residuals calculated by simulation from the fitted
model; and two further tools for comparing models, the Bayesian information criterion and
cross-validation. One example runs through the chapter, the functional response of
dragonfly larvae that prey on reed frog tadpoles (Vonesh and Bolker 2005).^[Vonesh, J. R.
and Bolker, B. M. (2005), "Compensatory larval responses shift trade-offs associated with
predator-induced hatching plasticity", *Ecology* 86: 1580–1591. The data are in the
package `emdbook`.] These are the data that Chapter 5 used as a backdrop and for which it
read starting values by eye. The observations are numbers of tadpoles killed out of a known
number, so the distributions of the chapter are the Binomial and the Beta-Binomial, and the
residuals are calculated with the package DHARMa. Every tank is treated as an independent
observation; [Chapter 7](../Chapter_7/Theory.qmd) extends the models to observations that
come in groups.

# Learning goals

In this chapter, we will cover:

- a response curve as a parameter of a distribution;
- the likelihood of a response curve and its fit;
- how RTMB calculates the gradient of the negative log-likelihood;
- standard errors, correlation and likelihood profile intervals of the parameters of a
  curve;
- the uncertainty of the fitted curve;
- simulation from a fitted model and scaled quantile residuals;
- a model for overdispersed proportions;
- model comparison with AIC, AICc, BIC and leave-one-out cross-validation.

We will use the [Binomial](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-binomial) and
[Beta-Binomial](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-beta_binomial) entries of the
distribution supplement and the
[Michaelis–Menten](../Supplements/deterministic-functions.qmd#sec-fn-michaelis-menten) entry
of the function supplement.

The table below is a roadmap of the chapter. Each row is one step, with the question that
it answers and the R tools that we use for it.

| Step | Question it answers | In R |
|---|---|---|
| The model | Which parameter of which distribution does the curve describe? | `plogis()`, `exp()` |
| The fit | Which parameter values make the observed counts most probable? | NLL with the predictor in the list of data, `MakeADFun()`, `optim()` |
| The gradient | How does the optimiser know in which direction to move? | `obj$gr()` |
| Uncertainty of the parameters | How precisely are the parameters of the curve estimated? | `sdreport()`, `cov2cor()`, `TMB::tmbprofile()`, `confint()` |
| Uncertainty of the curve | How precisely is the curve itself estimated? | `ADREPORT()` on a grid of the predictor |
| Checking the model | Does the fitted model describe the data? | `OBS()`, `obj$simulate()`, `DHARMa::createDHARMa()` |
| Revising the observation model | What if the counts vary more than the model allows? | `dbetabinom()` |
| Comparison | Which of the candidate models do the data support? | AIC, AICc and BIC from `fit$value`; a `for` loop that leaves out one tank at a time |

: Roadmap of the chapter.

# From a response curve to a model for observations {#sec-response-observation}

A **response curve** gives one parameter of the distribution of each observation as a
function of a predictor. Let $Y_i$ be the $i$-th observation and $x_i$ the value of the
predictor at which it was made. The parameter $\theta_i$ of its distribution is

$$
\theta_i=f(x_i;\boldsymbol\beta),
$$

where $f$ is a deterministic function of the kind studied in
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd) and $\boldsymbol\beta$ is the vector of its parameters
(the semicolon separates the input of the function from its parameters). Usually
$\theta_i$ is the mean, because the curves of Chapter 5 describe how an expected response
changes with a predictor. The other parameters of the distribution, such as the standard
deviation of a Normal model or the shape of a Negative Binomial model, are often shared by
all the observations. So every observation has a distribution of the same family, but with
its own value of the parameter that follows the curve.

The curve must return a value in the range of the parameter that it describes. A mean
count cannot be negative and a probability must lie between 0 and 1, whereas the functions
of Chapter 5 are not restricted in this way for every value of their parameters and of
$x$. The table gives the usual cases.
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-composition) showed how to give a curve
the range that a quantity requires, by passing it through an outer function.

| Distribution | Parameter that follows the curve | Range | How to give the curve that range |
|---|---|---|---|
| Normal | mean $\mu$ | any real value | any curve |
| Poisson, Negative Binomial | mean $\mu$ | positive | a curve that is positive for every $x$, or the exponential of another curve |
| Binomial | probability $p$ | between 0 and 1 | a curve between 0 and 1 for every $x$, or the inverse logit of another curve |

: Parameters that a response curve describes, and how a curve is given their range.

As in [Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd), we treat the observations as independent. They
are no longer identically distributed, however: two observations made at different values
of the predictor have different distributions, and the distribution of each observation
depends on the known value of its predictor. This is the change from Chapter 4, where every
observation had the same distribution. Note also that the observation model is a choice, in
the same way as the curve is (see "Choosing a distribution" in
[Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-discrete_distributions)), and in this chapter we
will revise it.

Let's write the model for the reed frog experiment. Sixteen tanks were stocked with
$N_i$ tadpoles, from 5 to 100, together with three dragonfly larvae, and $K_i$ is the number
of tadpoles killed in tank $i$ in 14 days. Each tadpole of a tank is either killed or not,
so we use a [Binomial](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-binomial) model with $N_i$
trials, in which the curve gives the probability that a tadpole is killed:

$$
K_i \sim \operatorname{Binomial}\left(N_i,\,p(N_i)\right),
\qquad
p(N)=\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha HN},
\qquad i=1,\ldots,16,
$$

where $\alpha$ is the attack rate and $H$ the handling time of the Holling type II form of
the disc equation ([Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-reparameterisation)). Here the
predictor, the initial number of tadpoles, is also the number of trials. The curve
describes the probability and not the number killed, because a Binomial distribution is
written in terms of the number of trials and a probability. The expected number killed is
then

$$
E[K_i]=N_i\,p(N_i)=\frac{\alpha N_i}{1+\alpha HN_i},
$$

the disc equation of Chapter 5. Under the assumptions of the disc equation, the probability
of being killed decreases with density because the larvae spend more of their time handling
the prey that they have caught. The
units follow from Chapter 5: the tadpoles killed were counted over the whole experiment,
so $\alpha$ is a fraction per experiment (at low density, a tadpole is killed with
probability close to $\alpha$) and $H$ is in experiments per tadpole killed. With
$0<\alpha<1$ and $H>0$, the probability $p(N)$ lies between 0 and $\alpha$ for every density,
so this curve has the range that the Binomial distribution requires without an outer
function; when we fit it, we keep $\alpha$ between 0 and 1 and $H$ positive with the
transformations of Chapter 4. We treat the 16 tanks as independent. The Binomial model also
assumes that, within a tank, every tadpole has the same probability of being killed,
independently of the others, which we check in @sec-response-residuals.

@fig-curve_distribution shows what the model says about the data, with the parameter values
that Chapter 5 read by eye ($\alpha=0.5$ per experiment and $H=1/60$ experiments per tadpole
killed). The curve gives the expected number killed at every density, and around it, at
each density, the Binomial distribution gives the probability of every possible number
killed. The spread of that distribution increases with the number of tadpoles in the tank.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-curve_distribution
#| fig-cap: "Number of tadpoles killed in each of the 16 tanks (points) against the initial number of tadpoles per tank. The line is the expected number killed under the Holling type II curve with the values read by eye in Chapter 5 (α = 0.5 per experiment, H = 1/60 experiments per tadpole killed). The horizontal bars show the Binomial probability of each number killed in a tank with 10, 50 and 100 tadpoles; their length is proportional to the probability."
# Reed frog functional response.
data(ReedfrogFuncresp, package = "emdbook")

# Expected number killed with the values read by eye in Chapter 5.
alpha_eye = 0.5
H_eye = 1 / 60
curve_eye = data.frame(initial = seq(from = 0, to = 100, length.out = 200))
curve_eye$killed = curve_eye$initial * alpha_eye /
  (1 + alpha_eye * H_eye * curve_eye$initial)

# Binomial probabilities at three densities, drawn as horizontal bars that start at the
# density. Probabilities below 0.002 are left out.
bar_scale = 40
mass_data = NULL
for (n_tadpoles in c(10, 50, 100)) {
  killed_values = 0:n_tadpoles
  p_eye = alpha_eye / (1 + alpha_eye * H_eye * n_tadpoles)
  probability = dbinom(x = killed_values, size = n_tadpoles, prob = p_eye)
  keep = probability > 0.002
  mass_data = rbind(
    mass_data,
    data.frame(
      initial = n_tadpoles,
      killed = killed_values[keep],
      probability = probability[keep]
    )
  )
}

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(
    data = mass_data,
    aes(
      x = initial, xend = initial + bar_scale * probability,
      y = killed, yend = killed
    ),
    colour = "#D55E00",
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = curve_eye,
    aes(x = initial, y = killed),
    colour = "#D55E00",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = ReedfrogFuncresp,
    aes(x = Initial, y = Killed),
    colour = "#0072B2",
    alpha = 0.7,
    size = 2
  ) +
  labs(x = "Initial number of tadpoles per tank", y = "Tadpoles killed in 14 days") +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {#imp-seedlings-light .callout-important title="seedlings and light"}

The number of tree seedlings in a quadrat is described with a Poisson distribution whose
parameter follows a curve of the light that reaches the soil, $x$ (% of full sunlight).
Which parameter of the distribution does the curve describe, and which values must it
return? Could the straight line $a+bx$ be used for every value of $a$ and $b$? Could the
Michaelis–Menten function $ax/(b+x)$ with positive $a$ and $b$, if some quadrats have no
light at all?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The curve describes the mean $\lambda$ of the Poisson distribution, the expected number of
seedlings per quadrat, which must be positive. The straight line becomes negative for some
values of $x$ unless $a$ and $b$ are restricted, so it cannot be used for every value of
its parameters; its exponential, $e^{a+bx}$, is positive for any $a$, $b$ and $x$. The
Michaelis–Menten function is positive for $x>0$, but it is zero at $x=0$. A Poisson
distribution with a mean of zero gives probability one to a count of zero, so a quadrat
without light that contains a seedling would have a probability of zero under the model,
and the log-likelihood could not be calculated.

:::
::::

# Fitting a response curve by maximum likelihood {#sec-fit-response}

The likelihood of a response curve is calculated as in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-likelihood): the observations are independent, so
the log-likelihood is the sum of the log probabilities (or densities) of the observations.
The difference is that each probability is calculated with the parameter of its own
distribution, which the curve gives at the predictor value of that observation:

$$
\ell(\boldsymbol\beta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\left(P(Y_i=y_i\mid\boldsymbol\beta)\right),
$$

where $y_i$ is the observed value of $Y_i$ and $P(Y_i=y_i\mid\boldsymbol\beta)$ is the
probability that the model assigns to it when the parameter of its distribution is
$f(x_i;\boldsymbol\beta)$ (any shared parameter of the distribution is added to
$\boldsymbol\beta$). Everything else is the same as in Chapter 4: we write the negative
log-likelihood (NLL) with two lists, transform the constrained parameters, connect the NLL
to the data with `cmb()`, process it with `MakeADFun()`, minimise it with `optim()` and
check the convergence. Two things are new. The list of data holds the predictor as well as
the response, and the starting values of the parameters of the curve are read from a plot
of the data, as in "Starting values by eye" in
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-starting-values).

For the reed frog tanks the log-likelihood is

$$
\ell(\alpha,H)=\sum_{i=1}^{16}\log\left(\binom{N_i}{K_i}\,p(N_i)^{K_i}
\left(1-p(N_i)\right)^{N_i-K_i}\right),
\qquad
p(N_i)=\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha HN_i}.
$$

We load RTMB and RTMBdist and the data of the experiment, and put the two variables that
the NLL uses in the list of data: `initial`, the number of tadpoles at the start of the
experiment in each tank (the predictor and the number of trials), and `killed`, the number
killed (the response):

```{r}
#| message: false
# Load RTMB first and RTMBdist second.
library(RTMB)
library(RTMBdist)

# Reed frog functional response (see ?emdbook::ReedfrogFuncresp): the initial number of
# tadpoles (Initial) and the number killed in 14 days (Killed) in each of 16 tanks.
data(ReedfrogFuncresp, package = "emdbook")
frog_data = list(initial = ReedfrogFuncresp$Initial, killed = ReedfrogFuncresp$Killed)
```

The NLL transforms the parameters, calculates the curve and adds up the log probabilities.
The attack rate is a probability, so the optimiser works with its logit, `logit_alpha`,
which `plogis()` turns back into $\alpha$; the handling time is positive, so the optimiser
works with its logarithm, `log_H`. Because `initial` is a vector, the line of the curve
returns a vector with one probability for each tank, and `dbinom()` uses the number of
trials and the probability of each tank:

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihood of the Binomial model with the Holling type II curve.
binomial_nll = function(parms, data) {
  # Make the elements of both lists available by name.
  getAll(parms, data)
  # Transform the parameters to the original scale.
  alpha = plogis(logit_alpha)
  H = exp(log_H)
  # Probability that a tadpole is killed, at the density of each tank.
  p = alpha / (1 + alpha * H * initial)
  -sum(dbinom(x = killed, size = initial, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
```

Chapter 5 read $a=60$ tadpoles killed and $b=120$ tadpoles per tank from a plot of these
data, which correspond to $\alpha=0.5$ per experiment and $H=1/60$ experiments per tadpole
killed. We give them to `MakeADFun()` on the transformed scales and fit the model:

```{r}
# Connect a likelihood to a data set.
cmb = function(f, d) function(p) f(p, d)

# Process the NLL, starting from the values read by eye in Chapter 5.
binomial_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(binomial_nll, frog_data),
  list(logit_alpha = qlogis(0.5), log_H = log(1 / 60)),
  silent = TRUE
)

# Minimise the NLL with BFGS and check the convergence code.
binomial_fit = optim(
  par = binomial_obj$par,
  fn = binomial_obj$fn,
  gr = binomial_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
binomial_fit$convergence
```

The estimates are transformed back to the original scale. By invariance
([Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-constraints)), the estimates of other quantities of
the curve follow from them. Two are useful here: the largest number of tadpoles that the
larvae could kill in one experiment, $1/H$, which is the asymptote of the expected number
killed, and the density at which the expected number killed reaches half of that
asymptote, $1/(\alpha H)$ (the parameters $a$ and $b$ of the Michaelis–Menten form):

```{r}
# Estimates on the original scale.
alpha_mle = unname(plogis(binomial_fit$par["logit_alpha"]))
H_mle = unname(exp(binomial_fit$par["log_H"]))

# Asymptote and half-maximum of the expected number killed, by invariance.
c(
  alpha_mle = alpha_mle,
  H_mle = H_mle,
  max_killed = 1 / H_mle,
  half_maximum = 1 / (alpha_mle * H_mle)
)
```

The estimates are $\hat\alpha\approx0.526$ per experiment and $\hat H\approx0.0166$
experiments per tadpole killed. The larvae could kill at most about 60 tadpoles in one
experiment, and the expected number killed reaches half of this at about 115 tadpoles per
tank. These values are close to the 60 and 120 that Chapter 5 read by eye
(@fig-fitted_curve), which is not surprising: the initial slope of the curve can be read
from the tanks at low density, and the asymptote that Chapter 5 chose happened to be close
to the estimate. Chapter 5 also found that these data say little about the asymptote, and
@sec-curve-uncertainty shows what this means for the uncertainty of the estimates.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-fitted_curve
#| fig-cap: "Number of tadpoles killed in each of the 16 tanks (points), with the expected number killed under the Binomial model with the Holling type II curve fitted by maximum likelihood (solid line) and with the values read by eye in Chapter 5 (dashed line)."
# Expected number killed with the maximum likelihood estimates and with the values by eye.
initial_values = seq(from = 0, to = 100, length.out = 200)
fitted_curves = data.frame(
  initial = rep(initial_values, times = 2),
  killed = c(
    initial_values * alpha_mle / (1 + alpha_mle * H_mle * initial_values),
    initial_values * alpha_eye / (1 + alpha_eye * H_eye * initial_values)
  ),
  curve = rep(c("Maximum likelihood", "By eye (Chapter 5)"), each = length(initial_values))
)

ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    data = ReedfrogFuncresp,
    aes(x = Initial, y = Killed),
    colour = "#0072B2",
    alpha = 0.7,
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = fitted_curves,
    aes(x = initial, y = killed, linetype = curve),
    colour = "#D55E00",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c("Maximum likelihood" = "solid", "By eye (Chapter 5)" = "dashed")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Initial number of tadpoles per tank",
    y = "Tadpoles killed in 14 days",
    linetype = NULL
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

A convergence code of zero is the first check of a fit. The next is whether the fitted
model describes the data, which we check with residuals in @sec-response-residuals. When the
code is not zero, the note "When a fit fails" in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-constraints) says what to try.

## The gradient and automatic differentiation {#sec-makeadfun}

Since [Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-maximum-likelihood) we have given every NLL to
`MakeADFun()` before fitting it. There we said that this step processes the NLL so that the
tools of the course can work with it, and that RTMB supplies the slope that BFGS uses. We
can now say what that slope is. The **gradient** of the NLL is the vector of its partial
derivatives with respect to the parameters
([Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-parameter-derivatives)), that is, its slope in the
direction of each parameter. RTMB calculates it by **automatic differentiation**: from the
code of the NLL, exactly up to rounding error, and without a formula from us. The element
`gr` of the object returns the gradient at the parameter values that we give it, on the
scale that is optimised, with one column per parameter in the order of the list of
parameters:

```{r}
# The gradient of the NLL at the starting values and at the estimates.
binomial_obj$gr(binomial_obj$par)
binomial_obj$gr(binomial_fit$par)
```

At the starting values the gradient is not zero, and its signs tell BFGS in which
direction to move each parameter to lower the NLL. At the estimates both elements are
close to zero, as they should be at a minimum.

An exact gradient matters for response curves for three reasons. First, BFGS uses the
gradient at every step to decide in which direction to move. Without `gr`, `optim()`
approximates it by evaluating the NLL at nearby values of every parameter
([Chapter 8](../Chapter_8/Theory.qmd) explains how), which costs time and accuracy. Second,
the parameters of a curve are often correlated, as we will see in @sec-curve-uncertainty,
so that the NLL forms a narrow and tilted valley like the one of the owl model in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-likelihood-surface). In such a valley the direction
of the next step depends on small differences between the partial derivatives, and an
inexact gradient can stop the search before it reaches the minimum. Third, the same
derivatives are behind the other tools of the course: `sdreport()` calculates the curvature
of the NLL from them, `ADREPORT()` uses them for the standard errors of quantities
calculated from the parameters (@sec-delta-method), and in
[Chapter 7](../Chapter_7/Theory.qmd) they are needed to integrate random effects out of the
likelihood.

For RTMB to calculate these derivatives, the NLL must be written with operations and
functions that RTMB knows. This is the reason why the probability mass and density
functions of the course come from RTMB and RTMBdist.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false title="Technical detail: how automatic differentiation works"}
[RTMB](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/RTMB/vignettes/RTMB-introduction.html) is an
R interface to the package Template Model Builder (TMB). `MakeADFun()` runs the NLL once, at
the starting values, and records every elementary operation that the function carries out on
the parameters (each sum, product, division, exponential and logarithm), in the order in
which they happen. This record is called a **tape**. The derivative of each of these
operations is known (they are the
[rules of differentiation](../Supplements/calculus.qmd#sec-calc-rules)), and the chain rule
combines them along the tape into the derivative of the NLL with respect to every parameter.
In plain English, RTMB differentiates the code of the NLL step by step, as we would
differentiate a formula by hand. The result is exact up to rounding error: it is neither an
algebraic formula nor a numerical approximation. The elements `fn`, `gr` and `he` (the
Hessian) of the object all work from the tape. Because the tape runs through TMB's compiled
code, it cannot be stepped through like ordinary R code.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="When automatic differentiation needs care"}
RTMB works out the derivatives from the calculations that the NLL carried out when
`MakeADFun()` ran it at the starting values. If the NLL contains a branch that depends on a
parameter (an `if` that compares a parameter with a value), only the side that was taken at
the starting values is used afterwards, and a curve with a sharp change at an unknown
threshold has no derivative at the change. Such
[calculations need special care](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/RTMB/vignettes/RTMB-tips.html).
Check the NLL on sensible parameter values in R first (a function written with `getAll()`
can be called directly with two lists), and inspect `binomial_obj$fn(binomial_obj$par)` and
`binomial_obj$gr(binomial_obj$par)` before fitting.
:::

# Uncertainty of a response curve {#sec-curve-uncertainty}

The uncertainty of the estimates is calculated from the likelihood, as in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-likelihood-uncertainty). Two questions are new
with a response curve. The first is how the precision of each parameter depends on where
the observations lie along the predictor. The second is how uncertain the curve itself is,
since a point of the curve is a quantity calculated from all of its parameters.

## Standard errors and correlation of the parameters

`sdreport()` calculates the standard errors and the covariance matrix of the estimates from
the curvature of the NLL, as in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-wald-automation). Two features are typical of the
parameters of a curve. Their estimates are often strongly correlated, because different
combinations of the parameters give similar curves over the range of the data. And how
precisely each parameter is estimated depends on where along $x$ the observations lie.
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-parameter-derivatives) showed with partial
derivatives that a curve responds to each parameter in a different part of its range; the
observations that inform a parameter are those made where the curve responds to it. So data
that cover only the rise of a saturating curve determine its initial slope better than its
asymptote. The correlation also depends on the parameterisation, whereas the fit does not
(see "Parameterisation, slices and profiles" in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-likelihood-surface)).

For the tanks, `summary()` gives the estimates and standard errors on the optimised scales,
and `cov2cor()` turns the covariance matrix in the element `cov.fixed` into correlations:

```{r}
# Standard errors on the optimised scales, and the correlation between the estimates.
binomial_sd = sdreport(binomial_obj)
summary(binomial_sd)
cov2cor(binomial_sd$cov.fixed)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
# The same model in the Michaelis–Menten form, with a = 1 / H and b = 1 / (alpha * H):
# the same maximum, and a higher correlation between the estimates of log(a) and log(b).
mm_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  a = exp(log_a)
  b = exp(log_b)
  p = a / (b + initial)
  -sum(dbinom(x = killed, size = initial, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
mm_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(mm_nll, frog_data),
  list(log_a = log(60), log_b = log(120)),
  silent = TRUE
)
mm_fit = optim(par = mm_obj$par, fn = mm_obj$fn, gr = mm_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
c(convergence = mm_fit$convergence, nll = mm_fit$value, nll_holling = binomial_fit$value)
exp(mm_fit$par)
cov2cor(sdreport(mm_obj)$cov.fixed)
```

The correlation between the estimates of $\operatorname{logit}(\alpha)$ and $\log(H)$ is
0.82. It is positive because a steeper initial rise of the curve (a larger $\alpha$) must
be compensated by a stronger levelling off (a larger $H$) for the curve to pass through the
tanks at high density, so hypothetical samples that overestimate one parameter tend to
overestimate the other. In the Michaelis–Menten form, with $\log(a)$ and $\log(b)$, the
same model has the same maximum and a correlation of 0.98: the estimates of the asymptote
and of the half-maximum are almost interchangeable, because the data determine mainly their
ratio, the initial slope $a/b=\alpha$. This is what Chapter 5 found when it read starting
values from these data ("Starting values by eye"). The densities of the experiment stop at
100 tadpoles per tank, below the estimated half-maximum of 115, so the tanks cover less than
half of the rise of the curve. They determine $\alpha$, which describes the start of the
curve, much better than $H$, which describes its end, as the intervals of the next section
show.

## Likelihood profile intervals of the parameters

Likelihood profile intervals are calculated with `TMB::tmbprofile()` and `confint()`, as in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-profile_intervals), and they remain the reference
method. With a response curve, the profile of a poorly determined parameter is often
asymmetric, because the data rule out values on one side of the estimate much more
strongly than on the other. The endpoints of the interval can be transformed with any
monotonic function to give an interval for a quantity calculated from the parameter: an
increasing function keeps their order and a decreasing function swaps them. We profile both
parameters, transform the endpoints back, and calculate the interval of the largest number
of tadpoles killed, $1/H$, from that of $H$:

```{r}
#| warning: false
# Profiles of logit(alpha) and log(H). Each profile contains the estimate twice, so
# confint() warns that it collapses repeated values; the warning can be ignored.
binomial_profile_alpha = TMB::tmbprofile(binomial_obj, name = "logit_alpha", trace = FALSE)
binomial_profile_H = TMB::tmbprofile(binomial_obj, name = "log_H", trace = FALSE)

# 95% intervals transformed back to the original scale.
alpha_interval = plogis(confint(binomial_profile_alpha))
H_interval = exp(confint(binomial_profile_H))

# 1 / H decreases with H, so the endpoints swap.
profile_intervals = rbind(alpha_interval, H_interval, rev(1 / H_interval))
dimnames(profile_intervals) = list(c("alpha", "H", "1/H"), c("lower", "upper"))
profile_intervals
```

```{r}
#| include: false
# Wald interval of H from the log scale, and the corresponding interval of 1 / H.
binomial_summary = summary(binomial_sd)
wald_H = exp(
  binomial_summary["log_H", "Estimate"] +
    c(-1, 1) * qnorm(p = 0.975) * binomial_summary["log_H", "Std. Error"]
)
rev(1 / wald_H)
```

The interval for the attack rate, 0.40 to 0.68 per experiment, is narrow compared with the
interval for the handling time, which spans almost a factor of four. Accordingly, the
interval for the largest number of tadpoles that the larvae could kill in one experiment
runs from 38 to 143 around an estimate of 60: it extends 22 tadpoles below the estimate and
83 above it, and its upper end lies beyond the largest density of the experiment. The data
rule out a low asymptote, because the larvae killed up to 35 tadpoles, but not a high one.
The profile is asymmetric even on the log scale, so the Wald interval from the log scale (34
to 107 tadpoles) misses most of the upper part of the profile interval.

## Uncertainty of the fitted curve {#sec-delta-method}

A point of the curve, such as the expected number killed at a given density, is a quantity
calculated from the parameters. Its standard error is requested with `ADREPORT()`, as in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-wald-constrained), where TMB applies the delta
method (the box below gives the formula for several parameters). `ADREPORT()` of a vector
reports every element with its own standard error, so if we pass a grid of predictor values
in the list of data and calculate the curve on that grid inside the NLL, `sdreport()`
returns the curve and its standard error at every point of the grid. From them we calculate
a Wald interval at each point, on a scale on which the quantity is unbounded, and transform
the endpoints back, for the same reasons as for the parameters in Chapter 4. For a
probability that scale is the logit. Together the intervals form a **confidence band**.

The band is **pointwise**: at each value of $x$, the interval contains the curve of the
model at that $x$ in approximately 95% of hypothetical samples. This is not the same as a
band that contains the whole curve in 95% of hypothetical samples, which would be wider.
The band also says nothing about where the observations of new tanks would fall: that is
described by the distribution of the observations around the curve
(@fig-curve_distribution), which is much wider.

For the reed frogs we add a grid of densities from 0 to 100 tadpoles per tank to the list of
data, as `initial_grid`:

```{r}
# A grid of densities (tadpoles per tank), added to the list of data.
initial_grid = seq(from = 0, to = 100, by = 1)
frog_data$initial_grid = initial_grid
```

The NLL gains three lines, which calculate the probability that a tadpole is killed at
every density of the grid, its logit with `qlogis()`, and ask for the standard error of
every element with `ADREPORT()`. We process the new NLL, fit it again (the estimates do not
change) and call `sdreport()`:

```{r}
# The Binomial NLL with three more lines.
binomial_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  alpha = plogis(logit_alpha)
  H = exp(log_H)
  p = alpha / (1 + alpha * H * initial)
  # The logit of the probability of being killed at every density of the grid.
  p_grid = alpha / (1 + alpha * H * initial_grid)
  logit_p_grid = qlogis(p_grid)
  ADREPORT(logit_p_grid)
  -sum(dbinom(x = killed, size = initial, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the new NLL, fit it again and calculate the standard errors.
binomial_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(binomial_nll, frog_data),
  list(logit_alpha = qlogis(0.5), log_H = log(1 / 60)),
  silent = TRUE
)
binomial_fit = optim(
  par = binomial_obj$par,
  fn = binomial_obj$fn,
  gr = binomial_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
binomial_sd = sdreport(binomial_obj)
```

With the argument `select = "report"`, `summary()` returns only the rows of the quantities
requested with `ADREPORT()`, here one row per density of the grid. We calculate the Wald
interval of each row on the logit scale, transform the endpoints back with `plogis()` and
multiply them by the density to obtain the band for the expected number killed:

```{r}
# Rows of logit_p_grid: one per density of the grid.
band_summary = summary(binomial_sd, select = "report")

# Wald intervals on the logit scale.
critical_value = qnorm(p = 0.975)
logit_lower = band_summary[, "Estimate"] - critical_value * band_summary[, "Std. Error"]
logit_upper = band_summary[, "Estimate"] + critical_value * band_summary[, "Std. Error"]

# The curve and its band for the expected number killed.
curve_band = data.frame(
  initial = initial_grid,
  killed = initial_grid * plogis(band_summary[, "Estimate"]),
  lower = initial_grid * plogis(logit_lower),
  upper = initial_grid * plogis(logit_upper)
)
```

@fig-curve_band shows the band with the data, the formula of the model and the estimates.
On the logit scale the band is narrowest in the middle of the densities of the experiment
and wider towards both ends, where fewer tanks constrain the curve. For the expected number
killed the band also widens with density because the probability is multiplied by the number
of tadpoles; at the highest density it runs from about 24 to 33 tadpoles killed. So within
the range of the data the curve is well determined, although its asymptote is not. Beyond
100 tadpoles per tank the band would widen quickly, because there the curve depends more and
more on the asymptote.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false title="Statistical detail: the delta method for several parameters"}
Let $g(\boldsymbol\theta)$ be a quantity calculated from the vector of parameters
$\boldsymbol\theta$ (on the scale that was optimised), such as the logit of the curve at one
density. Close to the estimates, the function $g$ is replaced by its tangent plane, the
extension of the tangent line of the one-parameter case to several parameters. The variance
of a linear function of the estimates follows from their covariance matrix, which gives

$$
\operatorname{Var}\left(g(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})\right)\approx
\nabla g(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})^{\top}\,\hat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}\,
\nabla g(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}),
$$

where $\nabla g$ is the gradient of $g$, the vector of its partial derivatives with respect
to each parameter ([Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-parameter-derivatives)),
evaluated at the estimates; $\hat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}$ is the covariance matrix of the
estimates, the element `cov.fixed` of `sdreport()`; and $^{\top}$ turns the column of
partial derivatives into a row. For two parameters the product is

$$
\left(\frac{\partial g}{\partial\theta_1}\right)^2\hat\sigma_1^2+
\left(\frac{\partial g}{\partial\theta_2}\right)^2\hat\sigma_2^2+
2\,\frac{\partial g}{\partial\theta_1}\,\frac{\partial g}{\partial\theta_2}\,\hat\sigma_{12},
$$

where $\hat\sigma_1^2$ and $\hat\sigma_2^2$ are the variances of the two estimates and
$\hat\sigma_{12}$ their covariance. In plain English, each parameter contributes its
variance multiplied by the square of the slope of $g$ in its direction, and each pair of
parameters contributes its covariance multiplied by the two slopes. With one parameter only
the first term remains, and its square root is the formula of the box on the delta method
in [Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-wald-constrained). For the curve of the reed frogs
a larger $\alpha$ raises the curve and a larger $H$ lowers it, so the two slopes have
opposite signs. Their estimates are positively correlated, so the last term is negative:
the two errors partly cancel on the curve, which is estimated more precisely than the
separate standard errors suggest.

RTMB calculates $\nabla g$ by automatic differentiation (@sec-makeadfun), which is why
`ADREPORT()` is called inside the NLL: the quantity has to be calculated there for RTMB to
differentiate it. The approximation is good when $g$ is close to a plane over the range of
parameter values that the uncertainty of the estimates covers. It is poor when $g$ bends
noticeably over that range, which happens when the standard errors are large (in small
samples) and when the quantity is close to a bound of its range on the scale on which it is
calculated; this is why the band is calculated on the logit scale.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-curve_band
#| fig-cap: "Number of tadpoles killed in each of the 16 tanks (points), with the expected number killed under the Binomial model with the Holling type II curve fitted by maximum likelihood (line) and its pointwise 95% confidence band (shaded), calculated from Wald intervals on the logit scale. The inset gives the model, the estimates and their 95% likelihood profile intervals; α is per experiment, H in experiments per tadpole killed and 1/H in tadpoles killed per experiment."
# Model, estimates and profile intervals for the inset.
format_interval = function(estimate, interval, digits) {
  paste0(
    formatC(estimate, format = "f", digits = digits),
    " [", formatC(interval[1], format = "f", digits = digits),
    ", ", formatC(interval[2], format = "f", digits = digits), "]"
  )
}
model_inset = paste(
  "Model: K ~ Binomial(N, p(N))",
  "p(N) = α / (1 + α H N)",
  "",
  "Estimates (95% profile intervals):",
  paste("α =", format_interval(alpha_mle, profile_intervals["alpha", ], 3)),
  paste("H =", format_interval(H_mle, profile_intervals["H", ], 4)),
  paste("1/H =", format_interval(1 / H_mle, profile_intervals["1/H", ], 1)),
  sep = "\n"
)

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = curve_band,
    aes(x = initial, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
    fill = "#D55E00",
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = curve_band,
    aes(x = initial, y = killed),
    colour = "#D55E00",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = ReedfrogFuncresp,
    aes(x = Initial, y = Killed),
    colour = "#0072B2",
    alpha = 0.7,
    size = 2
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    x = 0,
    y = 42,
    label = model_inset,
    hjust = 0,
    vjust = 1,
    size = 3.2,
    fill = "grey99",
    colour = "black",
    linewidth = 0.25
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 42)) +
  labs(x = "Initial number of tadpoles per tank", y = "Tadpoles killed in 14 days") +
  theme_classic()
```

Whether these intervals have a coverage close to 95% with 16 tanks can be checked by
simulation, in the same way as in "Coverage checked by simulation" in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-likelihood-uncertainty); the extra exercise of the
[practical](Practicals/no_solution.qmd) does this for a quantity of a fitted curve.

:::: {#imp-ladybird-handling .callout-important title="handling time of a ladybird"}

A Holling type II curve is fitted to the number of aphids eaten by ladybird larvae in one
hour, with the handling time $H$ (hours per aphid) optimised on the log scale. The fit gives
$\log(\hat H)=-3.2$, and `sdreport()` gives a standard error of 0.20 for it. Calculate a 95%
Wald interval for $H$, and from it an interval for the largest number of aphids that a
larva can eat per hour, $1/H$. Why are the endpoints swapped in the second interval?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

We calculate the interval on the log scale, transform its endpoints with `exp()`, and then
take the inverse of both endpoints:

```{r}
# Wald interval for H (hours per aphid), from the log scale.
H_wald = exp(-3.2 + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(p = 0.975) * 0.20)
H_wald

# Interval for 1 / H (aphids/hour): the inverse of the two endpoints, in reverse order.
rev(1 / H_wald)
```

The interval for $H$ goes from approximately 0.028 to 0.060 hours per aphid, and the
interval for the largest feeding rate from approximately 17 to 36 aphids/hour, around an
estimate of $1/e^{-3.2}\approx24.5$. The function $1/H$ decreases as $H$ increases, so the
lower endpoint of $H$ gives the upper endpoint of $1/H$, and the other way round. Because
the function is monotonic, the second interval contains $1/H$ in exactly the hypothetical
samples in which the first contains $H$, so it has the same coverage.

:::
::::

<!-- Stage 2 of Chapter_6/rewrite-handoff.md replaces everything below this comment. -->

# Compare candidate models {#sec-response-comparison}

An ecological question may support several curves. A Holling type II
([Michaelis–Menten](../Supplements/deterministic-functions.qmd#sec-fn-michaelis-menten))
function and a
[saturating exponential](../Supplements/deterministic-functions.qmd#sec-fn-monomolecular)
can both increase towards a plateau, but differ between low and high prey
density. Compare candidates that represent plausible explanations and use the
same observational unit and response. When one curve is a special case of
another, the two are nested, as described in
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-nested-functions).

## Information criteria

A model with more free parameters can often fit the observed data more
closely. Information criteria balance fit against model complexity.
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-aic) introduced the Akaike
information criterion (AIC); here we recall it and add the Bayesian
information criterion (BIC). For $K$ estimated parameters, $n$
observations and maximised log-likelihood $\hat\ell$,

$$
\mathrm{AIC}=2K-2\hat\ell,
\qquad
\mathrm{BIC}=K\log(n)-2\hat\ell.
$$

Both use the same fitted likelihood, but BIC's penalty per parameter
grows with sample size. Count observation-distribution parameters such as
$\sigma$ or a negative binomial shape parameter in $K$. On our `optim()`
fits, `intake_fit$value` is the *negative* log-likelihood, so
`2 * K + 2 * intake_fit$value` calculates AIC. A lower value is preferred by
that criterion **among the candidates compared**. The value does not
measure absolute model adequacy.

Only compare likelihoods computed for the same observed response on the
same scale, using the same rows and compatible probability masses or
densities. For example, dropping missing rows for one model but not
another makes an AIC comparison misleading. AIC and BIC can rank
misspecified candidates, so residual checks remain necessary. These
conditions also appear in [R's AIC documentation](https://search.r-project.org/R/refmans/stats/html/AIC.html).

::: {.callout-note title="What a small difference means"}
A small AIC or BIC difference gives little reason to claim that one
curve has a clearly preferable score. Neither criterion identifies a
biological mechanism or assigns a probability that a candidate is true.
:::

## Cross-validation

**Cross-validation** checks prediction on observations that were not used
to estimate a model's parameters. In five-fold cross-validation, divide
the observations into five parts. For each part, fit each candidate to
the other four parts, then score the held-out observations. Repeat until
every part has been held out once.

A useful score here is the sum of held-out log probabilities or densities.
It uses the whole predictive distribution, so it can assess continuous,
count, and binary models. Prefer the *larger* held-out log score. Refit
all parameters, including $\sigma$ or dispersion, within each training
set. Using the full-data estimates for held-out predictions would leak
information across the split.

Random folds suit observations that can reasonably be treated as
independent. For population measurements ordered in time, training on
later measurements to predict earlier ones answers a different question.
If the goal is future prediction, hold out later times and fit to earlier
times. [Time-based resampling guidance](https://rsample.tidymodels.org/articles/Common_Patterns.html)
uses this ordering for the same reason.

:::: {.callout-important title="Try it: score a held-out observation"}
A model assigns probability $0.8$ to a held-out species presence. Another
assigns probability $0.3$. Which model receives the higher log score
for this observation?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
The first: $\log(0.8)>\log(0.3)$. This one observation does not establish
which model predicts better across the whole dataset.
:::
::::

# Check the fitted observation model {#sec-response-residuals}

An ordinary residual such as $y_i-\hat\mu_i$ changes its meaning across
response distributions. It may also change its spread with the predictor
even when a count model is correct. **Simulation-based scaled quantile
residuals** provide a common scale: values between 0 and 1.

For each observation, simulate many possible responses from the fitted
model at its predictor value. Locate the observed response within those
simulations. An observation near the lower end gives a residual near 0;
one near the upper end gives a residual near 1. When the simulation
matches the observation process, the residuals should be approximately
uniform across 0 to 1 and show no systematic pattern against the
predictor. For discrete responses, randomisation handles ties. This is
the approach used by [DHARMa's scaled quantile residuals](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/DHARMa/html/getQuantile.html).

Our fits are ordinary `optim()` results, for which DHARMa does not know
the response distribution. We therefore generate a matrix with one row
per observation and one column per simulation, then supply it to
`DHARMa::createDHARMa()`:

```r
# Fix the random simulation sequence for a reproducible residual check.
set.seed(seed = 701)
# Calculate fitted means, then simulate complete intake measurements.
mu_hat = intake_curve(
  x = intake_data$x,
  a = estimates["a"], b = estimates["b"]
)
sigma_hat = estimates["sigma"]
simulated_rates = replicate(
  n = 500,
  expr = rnorm(n = nrow(intake_data), mean = mu_hat, sd = sigma_hat)
)
# Create scaled residuals from the simulations and plot them against density.
scaled = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = simulated_rates,
  observedResponse = intake_data$y,
  fittedPredictedResponse = mu_hat,
  integerResponse = FALSE
)
plot(scaled)
DHARMa::plotResiduals(scaled, predictor = intake_data$x)
```

Run this code after installing DHARMa in your R environment. For counts or
presence/absence, simulate with `rpois()` or `rbinom()` as specified by the
fitted model and set `integerResponse = TRUE`. The package's
[`createDHARMa()` documentation](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/DHARMa/html/createDHARMa.html)
describes this interface for custom simulations.

Look for a non-uniform residual distribution, a trend against $x$, changing
spread, or unusual concentrations near 0 or 1. For time measurements,
also plot against time in order. A diagnostic indicates where the model
disagrees with observations; it does not, on its own, tell us whether the
curve, observation distribution, dependence assumption, or data quality
caused the disagreement. Randomisation and a finite number of simulations
also make the exact plot vary between runs, so set a seed.

::: {.callout-warning title="What was simulated?"}
Simulate complete observations from the fitted distribution at each
predictor value. Simulating only the fitted mean curve produces no
observation-level variation and cannot support this residual check.
:::

# A fitting workflow

1. Plot the observations and check their units, support, missing values,
   repeated measurements, and predictor range.
2. Choose a small set of plausible mean curves and observation models.
3. Write the likelihood, check it at sensible parameter values, process it
   with `MakeADFun()`, fit every parameter, inspect convergence, and plot
   fitted curves against the data.
4. Estimate confidence intervals for ecologically meaningful parameters, and
   ask for quantities calculated from them with `ADREPORT()`.
5. Compare compatible candidates by AIC or BIC and, when appropriate,
   cross-validated predictive scores.
6. Simulate observations from the fitted model and inspect scaled
   residuals. Revise the model or qualify the conclusion when a pattern
   remains.

# Chapter quiz

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 1: the missing component"}
You have written $m(x)=ax/(b+x)$ and plotted it over the data. What must
you add before calculating a likelihood?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
Specify a distribution for observations around the curve, its remaining
parameters, and the dependence assumptions for the observational units.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 2: a positive parameter"}
Why might you estimate $\log b$ rather than $b$ directly? On which scale
should the final ecological interval be reported?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
Exponentiating an unconstrained estimate keeps $b$ positive. Calculate
the interval consistently on the fitted scale, then transform its
endpoints back to the units of the predictor.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 3: comparing models"}
Two models use different subsets of rows because only one removed
missing responses. Can their AIC values be compared as calculated?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
No. Fit both to the same observed responses and rows before comparing
their AIC values.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 4: held-out prediction"}
Why must an observation held out in cross-validation be absent from
*every* estimation step for its fold?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
Using it to choose parameters or dispersion would let information from
the assessment observation influence its own prediction.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 5: scaled residuals"}
A residual plot slopes upwards as the predictor increases. What can you
conclude, and what can you not conclude?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
The simulated model does not reproduce how the observations change with
the predictor. The plot alone does not identify which assumption or
ecological process caused that pattern.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 6: coverage"}
What must be known to estimate a confidence interval's coverage in a
simulation study, and why is this unavailable for an ordinary dataset?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
We must know the fixed generating parameter and repeat sampling and
interval construction. The generating parameter is unknown in an
ordinary dataset.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 7: automatic differentiation"}
What does RTMB provide to the optimiser, and why might a response curve with
an unknown sharp threshold need extra care?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
RTMB calculates the gradient of the NLL accurately by automatic
differentiation, and `optim()` receives it as `gr`.
At a sharp threshold the derivative may be undefined, and of a branch
chosen according to a parameter only the side taken at the starting values is
used. Check the NLL in R and consider a smooth curve or a different
fitting strategy for that model.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 8: the delta method"}
A fit gives $\log\hat b=2.40$ with a standard error of 0.11. What is the
approximate standard error of $\hat b$, and which line of the NLL makes
`sdreport()` report it?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
By the delta method it is the standard error on the log scale multiplied by
the slope of the exponential at the estimate, which is $\hat b=e^{2.40}\approx
11.0$: approximately $11.0\times0.11\approx1.2$, in the units of prey density.
The line `ADREPORT(b)` inside the NLL asks for it.
:::
::::
